newsitem.title: USA: US industry seen strong in Q3, autos are wild card.
newsitem.headline: US industry seen strong in Q3, autos are wild card.

text.p: Recent economic data hint the U.S. manufacturing sector is likely to remain fairly strong in the third quarter, with firms expected to partially re-build inventories to meet demand, experts said.

"My view is that these (recent) data suggest the manufacturing sector is accelerating, that growth is picking up ... from June and July's lows," said Richard Berner, senior vice president and chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
"The manufacturing sector might slow somewhat, but not until early next year," Berner added.
Analysts said expectations for steady consumer spending combined with rising salaries and wages could prompt companies to increase their inventories to meet the likely demand.
"Inventories are lean. Probably the gains in inventories in the quarter that we're in ... will be contributing to a faster pace of (industrial) growth," Berner said.

Recent economic statistics show the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) index rose to 52.6 in August against 50.2 in July. A reading above 50 suggests an expanding manufacturing sector.

The August employment report showed the economy added 250,000 new jobs in the month against am upwardly revised 228,000 in July. A closer look into the report also uncovered a strong rise in hourly earnings. The average hourly earnings component rose $0.06 to $11.87 from $11.81 in August.
On top of that, a new federal law increasing the minimum wage is also expected to put a couple of extra dollars into consumers' pockets.
The bill, signed by President Clinton in August, will boost the minimum wage by 50 cents to $4.75 on October 1 and by 40 cents to $5.15 on September 1, 1997.
In addition, analysts said recent strong orders in the aircraft sector could boost production in the third quarter.

"One sector that could provide some strength is aircraft. (Aircraft manufacturer) Boeing orders in recent months have been fairly strong," said David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
Analysts said, however, the auto sector remains the wild card when it comes to forecasting the country's manufacturing outlook.
Analysts said the possibility of an auto workers strike has cast a shadow over how the manufacturing sector as a whole will perform.
Some analysts said output could slow, while others did not discount the possibility of a surge in production as a pre-emptive move ahead of a possible strike.
"It seems like the auto companies are stepping up output probably in response to strong sales in the first half but also in anticipation of a possible strike," Sloan said.

Analysts said the United Auto Workers (UAW) union is expected to begin top-level negotiations on Monday with Ford Motor Co. The labor union appears to be putting the finishing touches on its bid to clinch a national labor agreement for the U.S. auto industry.

The current three-year pact between the auto makers and the UAW will expire Saturday. Analysts said negotiators are likely to try to trim the differences between their proposals during talks this week.
If no agreement is reached, auto workers have said they might enter a strike.
"Third-quarter production is very much up in the air because of the auto industry," said Peter D'Antonio, economist at Citicorp Securities Inc.
Some analysts cautioned, however, that the damaging effect of a possible strike should be short lived.

"The important thing to always remember about a strike is that it has a short-term impact ... that will be offset quickly when the strike is over," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.
